Snuff
snuf
v.i. & v.t. (to draw in air through the nose; to sniff at contemptuously)
Dutch snuffen, to snuff or sniff. The Authorized Version uses it of wild asses drawing in the wind in a drought, and — devastatingly — of priests sniffing in contempt at the altar of the LORD.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah twice paints the wild ass in the high places: she is “a wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away?” (Jeremiah 2:24), a figure for Judah's untameable appetite after other gods; and in the drought, “the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass” (Jeremiah 14:6). The picture is of a creature drawing in air because there is nothing else to take in. Malachi turns the same verb on the priesthood, and it is among the sharpest sentences in the prophets: “Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering” (Malachi 1:13). The men whose office was the altar had come to sniff at it as at a bad smell, and the blemished animals in their hands were the proof.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines snuff as to draw in with the breath through the nose; and figuratively, to snuff at, to express contempt by the nose.

expand to see more

SNUFF, v.t. To draw in with the breath through the nose; to inhale.

SNUFF, v.i. To snort; to draw air with violence up the nose; and figuratively, to express contempt.

SNUFF, n. The burning part of a candle wick, or that which has been charred by the flame.

WEARINESS, n. The state of being weary or tired; lassitude; that lassitude which is induced by exertion.

CONTEMPT, n. The act of despising; the act of viewing or considering and treating as mean, vile and worthless.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 2:24 — "A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away? all they that seek her will not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her."

Jeremiah 14:6 — "And the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass."

Malachi 1:13 — "Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering: should I accept this of your hand? saith the LORD."

Malachi 1:14 — "But cursed be the deceiver, which hath in his flock a male, and voweth, and sacrificeth unto the Lord a corrupt thing: for I am a great King, saith the LORD of hosts, and my name is dreadful among the heathen."

Modern Corruption

Boredom with worship is now excused as a matter of style and preference, when Malachi records God's own verdict on men who called his service a weariness and snuffed at it while still performing it.

expand to see more

The commonest modern account of a wandering heart in worship is that the form is at fault — the music, the length, the manner — and the remedy is presentation. Malachi 1 treats the same complaint as sin and names it exactly: what a weariness is it, and ye have snuffed at it. The offering was still being brought. Nobody had left; the sacrifices continued; the priests were at the altar. What God saw was the nose wrinkled at his own table, and what he pointed to as evidence was not their liturgy but their livestock: the torn, the lame and the sick, because a man who despises the worship gives God what costs him least.

Jeremiah's wild ass supplies the other half of the diagnosis and it is bleaker. A creature in a drought stands in the high place and snuffs up the wind because there is no grass; a creature in her occasion snuffs the wind at her pleasure and no one can turn her away. Appetite untamed and appetite unfed look almost identical from outside. The recovery is not a better atmosphere but repentance and a costly offering — and the assurance that the LORD of hosts, whose name is dreadful among the heathen, is worth a man's best animal and his undivided attention.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaaph (H7602), to gasp or snuff up; naphach (H5301), to blow or puff at; telaah (H8513), weariness; mashchath (H4893), a corrupt or blemished thing.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaaph (H7602) — to gasp, to snuff up the wind; the wild ass of Jeremiah 2:24 and 14:6.

Hebrew naphach (H5301) — to blow, to puff at in contempt; ye have snuffed at it.

Hebrew telaah (H8513) — weariness, hardship; what the priests called God's service.

Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to seize; the torn animals they brought instead.

Hebrew mashchath (H4893) — a blemish, a corrupt thing; the cursed deceiver's offering.

Usage

"“That snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure” — appetite no man can turn."

"“They snuffed up the wind like dragons” — because there was no grass."

"“Ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts” — contempt at the altar."
